https://www.smh.com.au/traveller/reviews.text: Advertisement Given the concern surrounding the routes of Middle Eastern airlines, I am considering fares with a cancellation policy. I notice most have a fee which I believe applies each way. Does this type of cancellation policy apply even if I change my mind, no reason required? S. Vlamis, Highton, Vic If considering travel via the Middle East, it makes sense to book a refundable ticket. AP The terms and conditions regarding flight cancellations vary depending on who you’ve booked through. If it’s a booking made directly with an airline, then a refundable or flexible fare generally allows you to cancel because you’ve changed your mind. However, the amount of the refund is determined by the fare conditions. A fully refundable fare will usually be from the most expensive category, but it does what the name suggests. Most other fare categories involve a cancellation fee. If you buy your ticket from an online travel agency such as Booking.com or Trip.com, it may come with a different set of conditions from the airline’s own fare rules, and these conditions are likely to be more stringent. Booking a refundable airline fare, either fully refundable or with a relatively small cancellation fee, is a sensible option. The fee you pay for cancelling a booking is a one-off fee that applies to the entire booking, it doesn’t apply to each of the outbound and return sectors of a journey. In December, my wife and I are looking at travelling by train from Tallinn to Warsaw. Is this doable, and do you have any useful tips? We are happy to stop over along the way, so any recommendations for cities to visit would be appreciated. M. Anderson, Epping, NSW Advertisement Tallinn, capital of the Baltic state of Estonia, from the tower of St Olaf’s. iStock Sign up for the Traveller newsletter The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now. The simplest route takes you from Tallinn to Warsaw via Riga and Vilnius. Travel time from Tallinn to Riga is six hours with no transfers on the fastest train. Riga to Vilnius is a four-hour journey and Vilnius to Warsaw takes more than six hours with one change. If it’s a case of either/or, Riga is a compact, elegant city with one of Europe’s finest collections of art nouveau architecture and a lively cafe and bar scene. A highlight is the enormous Central Market, housed in former Zeppelin hangars. A full day is enough time to take in the main sights. Vilnius is more appealing if you want to explore one of Europe’s largest surviving medieval old towns with fewer tourists, and enjoy its relaxed, bohemian vibe. You would need two to three days. The Man in Seat 61 has plenty of useful information on train travel in the Baltic States, including schedules and how to buy tickets. In February next year I’m taking a bucket-list trip to Antarctica. Any idea if expedition landings will be affected by bird flu issues? M. Cartwell, Blackburn, Vic While it’s unlikely that bird flu would cause you to miss your Antarctic landings, some specific landing sites may be changed at short notice. In response to the highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, the International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators, which governs virtually all expedition cruise operators, has introduced biosecurity and wildlife management protocols. Before every landing, expedition staff assess wildlife colonies for signs of avian influenza. If there’s evidence of disease or unusual mortality, that landing may be cancelled and replaced with another site or a Zodiac cruise. You can also expect enhanced biosecurity, with a high likelihood of disinfection baths for footwear after landings and a requirement to avoid sitting or kneeling on the ground and keeping well away from wildlife. Antarctic cruises are always subject to the changeable nature of the environment. Sea ice, weather and whales all have a bearing on day-to-day plans, but they do not usually negatively impact the experience. Advertisement I’d like to celebrate my 50th birthday in Italy with my husband and three children, aged 20, 18 and 15. I’ve been to Italy three times but this would be a first for my family. Can you suggest a two-week itinerary for July 2027? M. Costigan, Bentleigh, Vic Via Della Lungaretta in Trastevere, Rome. iStock Italy in July will be hot, crowded and expensive. For all those reasons I’d suggest visiting in May or after mid-September. You’ll probably fly into Rome, so spend a few days there taking in the city’s amazing sights. Balance the classic tourist spots with some neighbourhood life in Trastevere. There are plenty of fun things that the kids will enjoy, such as Vespa tours or a self-drive Fiat 500 tour. CitizenM Rome Isola Tiberina is a funky, design-forward hotel near the River Tiber, a perfect location for exploring both sides of the city, and the price is reasonable. Take the train to Bologna. It’s a sophisticated, open-air museum that feels authentic rather than overtouristed. Its large student population gives it a vibrant atmosphere as well as many low-cost dining options. Take a day trip to Modena to visit the Enzo Ferrari Museum; the one at Maranello on Modena’s outskirts is quite spectacular but more difficult to access. From there head for the Cinque Terre. Stay either at Monterosso or Vernazza and spend three days swimming in the Mediterranean off the rocks, hiking between gorgeous villages, enjoying the local seafood and gelato every afternoon. Advertisement Hire a car in La Spezia and spend three to four nights in an agriturismo in the Val d’Orcia, south of Siena. Spend your time exploring this very different side of Italy, taking in Pienza, Montepulciano, the small, family-operated wineries of the region and the farm restaurants. Drive to Orvieto, spend whatever time you have left here then take the train to Rome for your flight home. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The coroner’s office gave his cause of death as ‘blunt force injuries due to fall from height’. Photograph: Belle Chasse High School via Facebook View image in fullscreen The coroner’s office gave his cause of death as ‘blunt force injuries due to fall from height’. Photograph: Belle Chasse High School via Facebook New Orleans Teenager dies after falling in abandoned high-rise tower in New Orleans Jacque St Ann, 17, and his friends broke into Plaza Tower and he fell as they were descending an interior staircase Lucy Campbell in New Orleans Tue 18 Aug 2026 13.31 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 13.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A high school student recently fell to his death after entering an abandoned high-rise tower in downtown New Orleans with his friends – in an apparent case of urban exploration highlighting the dangers of unaddressed city blight. New Orleans police said Jacque St Ann, 17, and his friends, of the nearby community of Belle Chasse, Louisiana, traveled into the city and broke into the fenced-off, 45-story Plaza Tower in the central business district, which has stood derelict for years. They ascended to a higher floor at about midnight on 15 August – and Jacque fell to his death as they tried to descend an interior staircase. Citing respect for Jacque’s family, police declined to say from what floor he fell. Local paramedics pronounced Jacque dead at the scene. The coroner’s office gave his cause of death as “blunt force injuries due to fall from height”. Another in the group was hospitalized because of a deep laceration to an arm and wrist. Police did not disclose how many teens were in the group – and believe some may have left before Jacque fell. In the aftermath of the death, New Orleans police warned the public against “urban exploring” – which involves entering off-limits, abandoned structures. View image in fullscreen The Plaza Tower in New Orleans, Louisiana. Photograph: Khairil Azhar Junos/Alamy They said Plaza Tower’s darkness and deteriorating condition added to a situation that was already highly dangerous. “This is not a safe building, and this is not a safe place to poke around – and at night, and in the dark in the middle of the night,” Nicholas Gernon, a deputy police superintendent, said at a news conference. “This is truly a tragic incident – and so no one, kids or adults, should be entering into boarded-up, abandoned buildings, especially when they are secured. Let us make sure we offer our condolences and sympathies to this young man who lost his life,” said Michael Harrison, New Orleans deputy mayor, a former city police superintendent. Anne Kirkpatrick, a police superintendent, acknowledged how Jacque’s friends, along with his and their families, are “traumatized” – though she also invoked the possibility of trespassing charges after a grieving period. Furthermore, established urban explorers, who as a hobby enter abandoned or off-limits buildings to photograph and explore them have responded by discouraging young people from going into such structures, as Guardian news-gathering partner WWL Louisiana reported . They say the hobby is replete with physical dangers. Jacque’s death, meanwhile, has also prompted questions to the owners of Plaza Tower, which has been left to sit in dilapidation for years. The 58-year-old Plaza Tower has not been used since before Hurricane Katrina struck New Orleans in 2005. In 2021, debris falling from the building struck a passing cyclist, leading to the installation of protective netting at the site. City officials identified Alexandria Land & Development LLC – the estate of late New Orleans land magnate Joe Jaeger – as the owner. And they said that entity still has the legal responsibility to secure the privately owned building. Jaeger bought the Plaza Tower in 2014. But over the years a lack of action led the city to issue fines to Jaeger and obtain a court order for its demolition. It also attempted to work with him on redevelopment plans before his death in a car accident in June 2024. Meanwhile, potential sales of the building complicated the pathway to demolition, which would cost an estimated $25m to 28m. Redevelopment plans have also stalled amid struggles to secure financing. In a statement, the administration of the New Orleans mayor, Helena Moreno, pledged to continue taking steps to secure the safety and security of the building – as well as “working to support [its] the redevelopment … which will return Plaza Tower to commerce and will be essential to the long-term safety and vibrancy of the site”. The city said it also was still conducting a study to obtain a “Difficult to Develop Area” designation for the building, which would support the financing of a potential housing-related redevelopment. The mayoral administration’s statement said it “would like to see” the beginning of construction on such a project by the middle of 2027. Yet there was no immediate “specific timeline for redevelopment, or requirement to redevelop or demolish the property”, the mayoral administration said. “This is a privately owned property.” Additionally, New Orleans police said they would temporarily increase patrols around Plaza Tower. “The administration is in touch and has been in touch with the ownership. It is the owner’s responsibility to ensure that this abandoned building is secure and that no one can enter it. There have been issues in the past about the security of the building,” Harrison said. Kirkpatrick said that her “understanding is that there is security provided but I can’t tell you that it was there at the time because obviously the kids got in”. The owner could “possibly” face charges for failing to secure the property, she added, but that would be looked at a later date. A statement shared on Facebook on behalf of Jacque’s family said, “We miss our boy more than words could ever express. “Our hearts want nothing more than to have him back with us. We love him beyond measure, and that love will never end.” Jacque’s school, Belle Chasse high, said , “Jacque was an outstanding student and, more importantly, an exceptional young man who made a lasting impact on those around him … His absence will be felt deeply by … everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.” The school district which governs Belle Chasse high also said it would make counselors available for students and staff through the upcoming week. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The monitor’s report is based on a three-day visit to Villawood detention centre in March, when 428 people were being held, including children. Photograph: Torsten Blackwood/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The monitor’s report is based on a three-day visit to Villawood detention centre in March, when 428 people were being held, including children. Photograph: Torsten Blackwood/AFP/Getty Images Australian immigration and asylum Drug-dealing, makeshift weapons and a ‘culture of fear’ at Villawood detention centre, report warns Prolonged detention of children, insufficient staffing and hazardous damage to buildings are among the ombudsman’s concerns Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Doherty and Christopher Knaus Thu 20 Aug 2026 05.23 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 05.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Drugs are being openly dealt inside Villawood detention centre; makeshift weapons are being manufactured amid intimidation, standover tactics and a “culture of fear”; people are sleeping outside under CCTV cameras for their own safety; and children are being kept from going to school, a scathing report from the independent monitor has found. The commonwealth’s National Preventive Mechanism issued the report based on a three-day visit in March this year. A total of 428 people were held in Villawood at the time, including children. Some 78 beds were offline because of damage still not repaired from a fire three years ago. Those detained had been in detention for between two days and 11 years. Three people had been held inside Villawood for more than a decade. Escapes, fires, stabbing: catastrophic security failures revealed in Australia’s immigration detention network Read more Villawood has experienced consistent acts of violence and of self-harm, including numerous suicides . In January, a man died in the centre after being allegedly attacked by another detainee, who was subsequently charged with his murder. The commonwealth ombudsman identified key concerns including the prolonged detention of children, safety concerns, insufficient staffing, and the hazardous damage to buildings. People detained at Villawood also reported the “free movement” of drugs into and around the centre “alleging that substance use is commonplace and illicit substances are being traded relatively openly”. “People in detention expressed concern and fear about the use and trade of illicit substances within the facility and the effect this was having on their sense of safety. “They described incidents of aggressive behaviour, intimidation and standover tactics associated with the illicit drug market, which they perceived as contributing to a culture of fear within the centre,” the report said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Some people reported that people who had not used drugs before being detained had become drug users inside Villawood. The monitor found large shards of glass in common areas “a hazard in themselves but which could also be used as weapons”, as well as damage to concrete and brickwork “consistent with sharpening of metal objects, suggesting that some people in detention may be attempting to produce makeshift weapons”. People were sleeping outside, or in common areas, in Villawood detention centre. Some said they were sleeping outside because air conditioners had been broken and not repaired for months, and it was too hot inside rooms. “Others indicated that they chose to sleep in common areas rather than their assigned rooms, as they perceived these areas to be safer due to the presence of CCTV monitoring (noting that bedrooms are not monitored by CCTV in most accommodation compounds).” View image in fullscreen The ombudsman’s report warns the issues ‘require urgent remedial action to ensure the safety of people in detention, staff and to maintain the good order of the facility’. Photograph: Daniel Munoz/Reuters Particular concern was raised about children in a family group who had been detained for months but were isolated and being denied access to schooling. “There is a high risk that the continued detention of children … will be detrimental to their mental health, wellbeing and social and emotional development,” the NPM report said. “The absence of peer engagement and meaningful activities further compounds these risks.” The government says children in detention now have access to remote education. The NPM report also highlighted parlous staffing levels, exposing both workers and those detained to danger. During the visit, the NPM “directly witnessed an example of staff failing to intervene to prevent escalation of a serious physical altercation”. Previous lapses Insufficient staffing levels have been a consistent issue at Villawood. A Guardian Australia investigation has previously revealed that Comcare, the federal work safety regulator, issued a direct warning to the department that the “minimalist staffing model” employed by MTC, the US private prison company running detention centres , was endangering staff and detainees. The understaffing crisis is so bad that seriously ill detainees have been denied access to healthcare and large sections of Villawood have been left without a single staff member, in one case allowing a detainee to start a fire within a staff compound. Other security lapses have allowed the escape of high-risk detainees, caused ill-equipped staff to be stabbed and hospitalised, and prompted MTC to issue a since-abandoned edict that all detainees be handcuffed during escorts, regardless of their risk rating. Lawyers described that policy as “almost certainly unlawful”. The situation was deemed so serious that the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, hauled in the global president of MTC to dress him down for the company’s failures just six months after it began operating the centres on a $2.3bn contract . Urgent action required The Commonwealth Ombudsman, Iain Anderson, said conditions at Villawood represented a “failure to provide a level of services that meet minimum standards of safety, care and support”. “The issues observed at the Villawood Immigration Detention Centre require urgent remedial action to ensure the safety of people in detention, staff and to maintain the good order of the facility. If unaddressed, there is a risk of further deterioration in conditions and increased harm to people in detention and staff, potentially including serious injury and loss of life.” The acting secretary of the home affairs department, Hamish Hansford, responding to the report, wrote that “we recognise the importance of ensuring people in immigration detention are treated with dignity and respect, and of maintaining immigration detention arrangements that are safe, appropriate and consistent with Australia’s obligations”. The department agreed with eight of 15 recommendations from the ombudsman and partially agreed with the remaining seven. “In a number of instances, matters raised have already been addressed or are currently in progress,” Hansford wrote. “The report provides a useful opportunity to reflect on our practices and identify areas for continued improvement across immigration detention operations.” Explore more on these topics Australian immigration and asylum Migration news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘An insult’: Zomi Frankcom’s family issues strongly-worded statement as Israel rejects criminal investigation into her killing Nestory Irankunda says Pauline Hanson’s Socceroos monocultural claim made ‘us boys angry’ Impassioned Jacqui Lambie reveals health struggle as she condemns Labor’s ‘callous disregard for veterans’ One Nation wants to restrict migration. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/20/russ.text: Russians are casting their ballots on Sunday in the final day of voting in parliamentary elections, with the pro-Putin United Russia party widely expected to emerge victorious.United Russia has won every parliamentary election in the country since 2003.The 2026 vote marks the first since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, meaning it could offer a slight hint at public sentiment towards the conflict, which has been increasingly impacting Russians at home.However, in August, Russia's Supreme Court ordered the only party opposing the war - the Yabloko party - to be struck from the ballot. Its candidates are reportedly still able to run for individual seats in some districts.In a statement at the time, Yabloko cofounder Grigory Yavlinsky hit out at the decision and said they would appeal."Barring Yabloko from the elections means refusing to engage in dialogue with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities," he said. "We stand for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace, for the prevention of nuclear war".On Saturday, the party reported that one of its election observers had "lost consciousness" while being "subjected to force" by police in St. Petersburg. It also complained that party observers were being "denied access to polling stations" and that their movement was being "restricted."Russia reports cyberattacksElla Pamfilova, the chair of Russia's Central Election Commission, said on Sunday that Russia had recorded more than 1,000 waves of distributed denial-of-service attacks (DDoS) on election infrastructure over the last few days, per the Interfax news agency."The level of impact is assessed as very high," she said, adding that the attacks appeared to have been "carried out by highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools."A DDoS attack involves hackers attempting to disrupt a targeted network, server, or service by attempting to overwhelm the system with a large volume of traffic.Moscow hit by 'largest-scale attack'The vote comes as the Russian capital was hit by what its governor described as the "largest-scale attack" on the city since the war in Ukraine began.Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defences had shot down more than 1,600 drones across the country since Saturday, 450 of which he said had been heading towards the capital."Several drones reached the territory of the Moscow refinery, and one struck a residential building. There were no fatalities," he wrote. Moscow Oblast governor Andrey Vorobyov said two people had been killed in attacks across the wider region.Sobyanin also accused Ukraine of attempting to "disrupt" Russia's elections - which will determine the makeup of the 450-seat state Duma - with the attacks.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine had targeted the Moscow region overnight, saying a "key" oil industry facility as well as a logistics facility were hit."Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night," he wrote in a post on X, adding that Russia had launched over 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 19 missiles against Ukraine this week.

https://www.dw.com/en/middle-corridor-ca.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NvZS Freight rail cars carrying containers are loaded onto a ferry at the Port of Kuryk in Kazakhstan for transportation across the Caspian Sea. The port is a key hub on the Middle Corridor Image: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement On the morning of October 6, drones hit two commercial ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, sinking one of the ships and causing alarm and outrage in both Bulgaria and the European Union . The drone attacks come at a time when the EU is pushing for Bulgaria to become a key entry point for goods imported from Asia to the bloc via the trade route known as the Middle Corridor. The Middle Corridor, which the EU also refers to as the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, connects Europe and Asia. It begins in China and runs through Kazakhstan , Azerbaijan , Georgia and Turkey before reaching the EU. Although it is mostly made up of railways and roads, short sections of the corridor cross the Black and Caspian Seas . Bulgaria and the Middle Corridor The EU has this year declared its intention to bet big on this trade route, a move that could affect Bulgaria's railways, roads and ports. Bulgaria's land border crossing with Turkey, Kapitan Andreevo, is already one of Europe's busiest, trucks frequently lining up at the checkpoint. The country also has two strategic ports on the Black Sea — Varna and Burgas — and a new section of a railway line between Istanbul and the Bulgarian border is set to open this fall. In September, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos called Bulgaria "Europe's Connectivity Gateway" due to its strategic location on this route. Wars have disrupted global trade routes A few months earlier, Kos said the Middle Corridor could considerably cut transport times from Asia to Europe from 45 days to just 15 days and is safer than the two traditional routes for goods being transported to Europe from Asia. One of these was an overland route via the Northern Corridor through Russia. Trade along this route dropped sharply after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . The other route, sometimes referred to as the Ocean Route, sees goods traveling by ship through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. But fears of disruption caused by wars and instability in the Middle East mean that many goods are now being shipped all the way around Africa — a journey that takes around 45 days. That results in delays and costs for businesses and consumers alike. All of this explains why the Middle Corridor suddenly seems so attractive — a fact confirmed by Vessela Tcherneva, deputy director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, who is based in Sofia, Bulgaria. "The Middle Corridor is a project that basically avoids both war theaters that we have near Europe," Tcherneva told DW. "It avoids the route through Russia , and also it avoids the route through the Middle East." Is the Middle Corridor a realistic alternative? As promising as it sounds, a lot needs to change before the Middle Corridor can really compete with the Ocean Route. "You have, first and foremost, security limitations," said Tcherneva. "The security situation in Central Asia needs to really have improved enough so that one can make long-term plans for constructing big projects." Tcherneva also stressed that weak institutions and bureaucracies in countries along the Middle Corridor are an issue. Russian involvement cannot be ruled out. "We have seen infrastructure projects in the past not happen because they were not perceived as being in Russia's interest, and the Russians seem to have quite a bit of leverage in the countries along the route," she said, adding that "the outcome of Russia's war in Ukraine is going to have an impact on the success or failure of the Middle Corridor." Tuesday's drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea are a stark reminder that security on the route could well remain a problem. In addition, the water level in the Caspian Sea, which is situated on the Middle Corridor, is falling , with climate change as a key driver. This means there is no guarantee that ships will be able to cross it in the future. EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos called Bulgaria 'Europe's Connectivity Gateway' due to its strategic location on the Middle Corridor Image: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/picture alliance Then there is the problem of infrastructure: Ports and railways along the route lack capacity for big increases in trade volumes. How Bulgaria could benefit Despite these risks and limitations, the EU clearly wants to see more trade coming through the Middle Corridor, even if it cannot replace existing routes. In her recent State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU wants to improve what it calls "connectivity." It wants to diversify trade routes, increase trade flows and reduce freight transit times. To do so, it aims to raise €12 billion ($13.5 billion) in public and private investment. Bulgaria could benefit from this in a number of ways. "The Bulgarian railways have been underinvested in for many, many years now — for decades. Bulgarian ports would also benefit greatly from investment," Tcherneva told DW. "Developing better road connections from the Mediterranean up, but also east-west, would help, especially the north of the country, which is currently not very well connected. So, there are clear benefits."
